v0.4.0 was about what you can see without asking. This one is about changing what you already made: fufu learns to rewrite history, and it learns it as one engine rather than six verbs that each grew their own.

**One engine, and plans that are not yet real**

Every rewrite in this release aims at the same place. A plan applies a change to a target commit, re-parents everything between it and the tip, and writes the objects while moving no refs — so the caller decides whether a plan becomes real. That is the whole reason `ff absorb`, `ff lift`, `ff describe <rev>`, `ff edit`/`ff done`, `ff restack` and `ff sync` share one implementation instead of six.

Merge commits are re-parented rather than refused. Rebase semantics for a merge are ambiguous, which is why the futures probe bails on them, but re-parenting one is not — and only commits actually descending from the target are rewritten, so naming a root commit does not drag in an unrelated line that was merged alongside it.

No empty commit survives a replay. A commit whose tree matches its new parent's introduces nothing, so it is dropped and named rather than written as an empty. `ff commit` refuses to make one in the first place, and `ff lift` drops a commit it would have emptied instead of leaving it behind. The rule is the same in all three places, which is what lets the next verb rely on it.

**The short reach**

`ff absorb` folds what is open into a commit that has already closed. `ff lift` takes it back out. Both take paths, and both take `--into` / `--from` to aim at a commit further back than the one under you.

Neither verb writes a file. Content is only reattributed between the open change and a commit, so the working tree after is byte-identical to the working tree before — and the tests check that by checksumming every file rather than trusting the claim.

`ff describe` grew the same reach. Given a revision it rewords a commit that has already closed, and everything above it re-parents in the same operation, so branches sitting inside that range come along.

**The primitive**

`ff restack` replays a branch's commits onto the base it sits on. The positional names a branch to move and `--onto` names where it lands and records it as that branch's new parent — which makes this the first rewrite verb you can point at a branch you are not standing on.

That turns out to be the simpler half rather than an extra one, and the whole implementation is organized around one rule: the working tree moves if and only if the branch HEAD stands on is one the rewrite carries. Always so for the branch you are on. True off-branch only when you are parked mid-stack inside the range, which is exactly when your tree should move. Never otherwise — and the differential proves that "never" by checksumming every file across an off-branch restack.

**Sessions, for when a diff is not enough**

`ff edit <rev>` opens an editing session on a commit: a branch is minted there and you switch to it, so the commit's real content is what you edit, with your whole toolchain pointed at it. The branch you came from stays where it stands with its commits waiting ahead, and your open change parks where you stood and comes back when the session ends.

`ff done` amends the commit with what you changed and replays what waited onto it. `ff done --abandon` drops the session instead. Handing `ff edit` a branch name is a switch rather than a session — the one available reading is taken, and announced.

**Conflicts on your schedule**

A rewrite that would conflict does not interrupt you. It is *held*: recorded on the branch as the verb's own question — the branch, the target, what it was asked to become — never as the plan it could not finish computing.

That distinction is what makes revalidating a hold a recomputation rather than a comparison. Nothing has to be pinned, because every input is a ref or the working tree. A pending rewrite replaying over whatever you add next costs nothing, because the replan sees what you added. A target that has gone expires the hold the moment somebody asks. And if the world moved such that the rewrite now applies cleanly, the hold is simply released.

`ff resolve` is where you choose to deal with it, all at once: every surviving conflict region lands in the working tree together as ordinary labeled markers, in one session. Fix them, and `ff done` lands the rewrite behind them. Nothing moves while you do it — not your branch, not the parked change. `ff resolve --abandon` drops the hold and an open session's markers with it, and either way the way back is one `ff undo`.

One hold per branch. A second *conflicting* rewrite refuses rather than guessing an order; one that would land cleanly is not competing for anything and goes through.

**Lining up, and publishing**

`ff sync` lines a branch up with both things it answers to — the base beneath it and the remote copy of itself — and publishes. One verb, because reconciling with either is the same replay, and publishing is the outgoing half of lining up rather than a separate act. There is no `ff push`. `fufu.pushOnSync` (default true, `--push`/`--no-push` per call) is the one knob, and `--no-fetch` reconciles with what you already have.

What that knob never buys is passage. The exit guards are properties of publishing rather than a mode, so a held rewrite refuses the push whichever way it is set.

The one question two axes cannot answer on their own is whose divergence it is. After any restack your branch diverges from its remote — and so does a branch a collaborator pushed to. Same shape, opposite correct answers, and getting it backwards either replays your rebased commits onto their stale originals or force-pushes over somebody else's work.

The rule: divergence this run's fetch created is theirs; divergence your own operation log accounts for is yours; anything else is theirs too. The middle clause is a lookup rather than an assumption — every commit the remote has and you do not has to appear in the log as the `old` side of a rewrite fufu recorded, or as one a replay dropped as empty.

The third clause is why the second is checked. Their commits reach the tracking ref through *any* fetch — an editor's background one, a manual `git fetch`, an earlier sync that fetched and then held — and by the time your sync runs there is nothing new to bring. Reading that silence as "the divergence is mine" would force-push over their work under a lease that cannot catch it, because the lease expects exactly the tip the remote already holds. Anything the log does not recognize replays instead, which never loses work.

**Smaller things**

Standing on trunk in a clone no longer produces two axes out of one ref. `origin/HEAD` names trunk, so trunk resolves to `refs/remotes/origin/main`, and comparing full ref names called that a different branch from local `main` and handed `main` its own shared copy as a base. Trunk identity is by name now — the identical test for a local trunk, and the right answer for a remote-only one. It also settles an asymmetry that had nothing to do with the display: `ff restack` on trunk used to refuse in a local-only repository and replay onto the remote copy in a clone. It refuses in both now, and `ff sync` is the verb that reconciles trunk with its remote.

`ff status`'s parent row names the capture it was cut from, instead of drawing the no-anchor glyph. `ParentStatus` had no field to fill, which made it a model fix rather than a rendering one: `ff status --json` carries the segment as hex like every other id in that model, and the human row prints the same letters `ff log` does.

`ff explain` grew from 58 error ids to 86 alongside the new verbs, so a refusal from any of them can be looked up by id.

1043 tests, up from 764 at v0.4.0 — including differential suites that check each new verb against the git recipe it corresponds to, byte for byte.
